repairs.why: FORBIDDEN_BY_LEDGER C12: 10 km/day presented as growing error; owner flagged
repairs.before: And the clocks involved are strange: the ones on the satellites run faster than yours. Einstein explains why, and engineers estimate that without the fix, errors would grow by roughly ten kilometers a day.
repairs.after: And the clocks involved are strange: the ones on the satellites gain thirty-eight microseconds a day on yours. That is thousands of times more than navigation can tolerate, and Einstein explains why.

repairs.why: FORBIDDEN_BY_LEDGER C12 and unmapped number 300 m
repairs.before: Thirty-eight microseconds sounds tiny, but a signal travels three hundred meters in one. Engineers estimate that, uncorrected, the errors would grow by roughly ten kilometers every day.
repairs.after: Thirty-eight microseconds a day sounds tiny. But a ranging error of three meters takes only ten nanoseconds of clock error. So the offset is thousands of times too big to ignore.

repairs.why: owner: do not equate satellite clock offset, pseudorange bias and position error; SRC24 (Misra) says position unaffected, timing affected
repairs.after: Here is the twist. Had engineers ignored relativity, every distance would come out too short by the same amount, up to about eleven kilometers. In this simplified picture the receiver would absorb that shared error into its own clock bias, and your position would survive. GPS time would not: it would be off by thirty-eight microseconds a day.

repairs.why: align with SRC24 (45 ns, +-15 m at e = 0.02); keep SRC5 as second source
repairs.before: Even then, orbits are slightly oval, so receivers apply one final relativity correction themselves. For a slightly oval orbit it reaches about twenty-three nanoseconds, roughly seven meters.
repairs.after: Orbits are not perfect circles, so a smaller relativistic error is left over, and it differs from satellite to satellite. For a slightly oval orbit it can reach about forty-five nanoseconds, roughly fifteen meters of range error, and receivers correct for it.

repairs.why: SRC24 now supports the receiver-clock statement; previous wording was hedged

repairs.why: owner: check C/A ambiguity and navigation message timing; now sourced to LNAV structure (SRC14)
repairs.before: The pattern repeats every millisecond, about three hundred kilometers of signal, so the message also carries a time count that tells the receiver which repeat it is hearing. With the orbit data in the message, each satellite becomes one sphere.
repairs.after: The pattern repeats every millisecond, about three hundred kilometers of signal, so the code alone fixes the delay only within one millisecond. The message supplies the rest: at fifty bits a second, each six-second block begins with a time-of-week word, so the receiver can work out which millisecond it is hearing.

repairs.why: owner: do not equate URE with smartphone accuracy; SRC16 defines URE as ranging accuracy and user accuracy as a position radius
repairs.before: That is why the satellites' accuracy and yours differ. The government commits to a signal error of at most two meters, and measured under one meter on one day in 2021. Phones typically get within about five meters under open sky.
repairs.after: Accuracy comes in layers. The satellites' signal is held to an error of at most about two meters, ninety-five percent of the time, and on one day in 2021 it averaged under one meter. But that is the error of one distance. Your position also depends on satellite geometry, the atmosphere and nearby buildings, so phones typically land within about five meters under open sky.

repairs.before: The ionosphere changes with the time of day and with solar activity. It delays lower frequencies more, in proportion to one over the frequency squared. So a receiver listening on two frequencies can compare the delays and correct for it. With the newer civil signal L2C, civilian receivers can do exactly that.
